agogwe|Capt. William Hichens' account of.summary: In the December 1937 issue of the journal Discovery, Captain William Hichens wrote that while waiting for a man-eating lion near the Wembere plains he saw two small, upright, russet-haired figures about 4 feet tall cross a forest glade. His guide called them agogwe. No physical evidence was ever found, and Hichens himself allowed that he may have seen monkeys.

ahool|Bartels sighting on Mount Salak.note: Only found in cryptozoology retellings (Coleman & Clark, Sanderson) and fan sites; no Wikipedia article, newspaper, museum or publisher page that I could open confirms Ernst Bartels' 1925 Mount Salak sighting.

ahool|Bartels hears the call again.note: Same as the 1925 case: the 1927 Tjidjenkol River account appears only in cryptozoology retellings and fan wikis; no reliable source I could open.

alien-abduction|Villas Boas case.summary: Brazilian farmer Antônio Vilas-Boas said that on 15 October 1957, while ploughing at night near São Francisco de Sales, an egg-shaped craft landed and short humanoids in grey coveralls seized him and took him aboard. A doctor, Olavo Fontes, interviewed and examined him in 1958. Skeptics suggest a hoax, but he reportedly kept to his story all his life.

alien-abduction|Betty and Barney Hill.summary: Betty and Barney Hill said that while driving home through rural New Hampshire on the night of 19-20 September 1961 a strange craft followed their car and they later had a gap of 'missing time'. Under hypnosis they described being examined aboard a craft. Their story became the 1966 book The Interrupted Journey; a state historical marker now stands near the site.
alien-abduction|Betty and Barney Hill.source_title: Barney and Betty Hill incident - Wikipedia

alien-abduction|Pascagoula abduction.summary: On 11 October 1973 Charles Hickson and Calvin Parker told the Jackson County sheriff that while fishing on the Pascagoula River they were taken aboard an oval craft by three creatures with 'pincers' and examined. Officers secretly recorded them alone and their story stayed the same. Skeptic Philip Klass concluded it was a hoax; the case remains disputed.

alien-abduction|Travis Walton disappeara.summary: On 5 November 1975 a logging crew near Heber, Arizona, said their co-worker Travis Walton was struck by a beam of light from a glowing object and vanished. He reappeared five days later saying he had been aboard a craft. Skeptics including Philip Klass argued it was a hoax to escape a late forestry contract; the story became the 1993 film Fire in the Sky.

almas|Zana of Abkhazia.summary: Local legend says a hair-covered 'wild woman' named Zana was captured in the forests of Abkhazia in the mid-1800s and lived out her life in the village of Tkhina. Soviet researcher Boris Porshnev collected the stories and believed she was an almas. DNA from a skull exhumed in 2021 showed Zana was a human woman of mostly African ancestry, possibly with a condition causing excess hair.

altamaha-ha|Wolf Island carcass stunt.summary: In 2018 a strange, decomposing carcass found on a beach in the Wolf Island National Wildlife Refuge set off talk that the Altamaha-ha had finally turned up. Performance artist Zardulu later said she made it as a prank from a stuffed shark and papier-mâché.

amabie|Amabie said to appear and foretel.summary: A woodblock print dated 1846 says a glowing creature with long hair, a beak and scales rose from the sea off Higo Province (today Kumamoto) and told an official that if disease spread, people should show its picture to the sick. The print, kept at Kyoto University Library, is the only early record of the amabie, which became a popular good-luck image again during COVID-19.

amomongo|Two men clawed and livestock ki.summary: On 9-10 June 2008, residents of a settlement in La Castellana, Negros Occidental, reported that a hairy, man-sized creature with long nails scratched two men and killed goats and chickens. Medical records noted scratches on the men. Scientists consider the amomongo a local legend mixed with mistaken identity.

barghest|Ballad of the Troller's Gill ba.summary: William Hone's Every-Day Book (1830) printed the ballad 'The Legend of the Troller's Gill', in which a man goes to the limestone gorge in the Yorkshire Dales to summon the barghest, a spectral black dog. He is found dead the next day with strange marks on his chest. It is a literary folk ballad, not a witness report.

barmanou|Magraner's team hears unexplain.summary: In May 1994 Spanish-born zoologist Jordi Magraner and his team, searching the Shishikoh valley in Chitral for the barmanou, said they heard unusual guttural calls late one evening. It was too dark to follow the sound to its source and nothing was found. Magraner, who collected dozens of local sighting stories, was killed in Afghanistan in 2002.

batsquatch|Brian Canfield encounter.note: Story (April 1994, Pierce County, WA; Tacoma News Tribune article by C.R. Roberts, 24 Apr 1994) appears only on blogs, fan wikis and radio-station listicles; the original newspaper article is not online and I found no reliable source to open.

bear-lake-monster|Deseret News articles.summary: In 1868 Joseph C. Rich, a settler in the Bear Lake valley, wrote in the Deseret News that a serpent-like 'water devil' known from Native tradition had been seen by several settlers. The stories caused a stir and other papers mocked them. Rich later admitted the story was 'a wonderful first-class lie'.

beast-of-bladenboro|First dog killed.summary: On 29 December 1953, witnesses described a sleek black animal about 5 feet long that killed a dog in Clarkton, North Carolina, about eight miles from Bladenboro. More dogs were found torn apart over the next days, which began the Beast of Bladenboro scare. Trackers thought it was probably a wild cat, but it was never confirmed.

beast-of-bladenboro|Mass hunt in Bladenb.summary: In early January 1954, after more animal deaths and heavy press coverage, crowds of armed hunters poured into Bladenboro to track the beast. On 13 January a farmer shot a bobcat caught in a trap and the mayor declared the beast dead, though accounts conflict and the animal behind the attacks was never firmly identified.

beast-of-bodmin|Ministry of Agriculture.summary: After years of reported big-cat sightings and livestock kills, the Ministry of Agriculture had the consultancy ADAS investigate Bodmin Moor in 1995. It found photos showed domestic cats, casts came from ordinary cats and a dog, and kills showed no sign of big cats, though it said it could never prove no such animal existed.
beast-of-bodmin|Ministry of Agriculture.source_title: Cat's out of the bag? - Dr David Clarke

beast-of-bodmin|Leopard skull found in t.summary: Shortly after the 1995 government report, a large cat skull with long canines was found in the River Fowey and offered as proof of the Beast of Bodmin. The Natural History Museum in London found it came from a real leopard, but one that had been cut from a leopard-skin rug, not an animal that lived on the moor.

beast-of-bray-road|Endrizzi roadside sig.summary: Lori Endrizzi said that in autumn 1989, at about 1.30 a.m., she saw a wolf-like animal with human-like features kneeling at the side of Bray Road near Elkhorn, Wisconsin. Her account was one of the first collected by reporter Linda Godfrey. Skeptics suggest witnesses saw wolves or large dogs.
beast-of-bray-road|Endrizzi roadside sig.source_title: Werewolves in America; the Tale of Dogman - Tetrapod Zoology

beast-of-bray-road|Gipson Halloween enco.summary: Doris Gipson said that on Halloween night 1991 she hit what she thought was a small animal on Bray Road, and when she got out to look, a large dark creature ran at her. Her report, together with earlier ones, led reporter Linda Godfrey to break the Beast of Bray Road story in late 1991. No physical evidence was found.
beast-of-bray-road|Gipson Halloween enco.source_title: Werewolves of Elkhorn - Time Out Chicago

beast-of-bray-road|Godfrey's book The Be.summary: Linda Godfrey, who covered the sightings for the Walworth County Week, turned her reporting into the 2003 book The Beast of Bray Road: Tailing Wisconsin's Werewolf. Starting as a skeptic, she came to believe many witnesses were sincere. The book helped make the creature part of Wisconsin folklore, while skeptics point to wolves or large dogs.

beast-of-busco|Oscar Fulk sighting.summary: In 1898 farmer Oscar Fulk said he saw a giant turtle in a seven-acre lake on his farm near Churubusco, Indiana. He told others about it but eventually stopped pursuing it. The turtle was later nicknamed Oscar after him.

beast-of-busco|Fishermen sighting.summary: In July 1948 two local men fishing on the same lake, by then called Fulk Lake, reported a huge turtle they guessed at about 500 pounds. Farmer Gale Harris, who owned the land, and others also said they saw it, and interest in the creature began to grow.

beast-of-busco|Lake drained in turtle hu.summary: In 1949 a wire story made the Churubusco turtle national news and crowds came to Gale Harris's farm. Harris tried to drain the lake and a diver was brought in, but the dam broke and the turtle was never caught. The town still holds Turtle Days each June.

beast-of-exmoor|Sheep killings and Royal.summary: In 1983 a South Molton farmer said he lost more than 100 sheep in three months to throat wounds, and the Beast of Exmoor became national news. The Daily Express offered a reward for footage and the government sent Royal Marine snipers to hunt it. No big cat was ever found; the kills are now generally put down to other causes such as dogs.

beast-of-gevaudan|First recorded victim,.summary: On 30 June 1764 a 14-year-old girl, Jeanne Boulet, was killed near Les Hubacs, close to Langogne. Her burial record blamed 'the ferocious beast', making her the first officially recorded victim of the Beast of Gévaudan. Attacks across the region over the next three years killed dozens of people.

beast-of-gevaudan|François Antoine shoot.summary: On 20 or 21 September 1765 François Antoine, the king's gun-bearer, shot a very large grey wolf near the Abbey of Chazes. It was stuffed and taken to Versailles, where Antoine was hailed as a hero, but attacks resumed a few months later.

beast-of-gevaudan|Jean Chastel ends the.summary: On 19 June 1767 local hunter Jean Chastel shot a large wolf-like animal on the slopes of Mont Mouchet. The attacks stopped afterwards, and Chastel was credited with killing the Beast of Gévaudan. Historians still debate whether it was one or several wolves, or another animal.

big-bird|Harlingen New Year sighting.summary: On New Year's Day 1976 two girls said a five-foot-tall bird with a strange face stared at them in their yard, and their parents found large three-toed tracks the next day, which were shown on local TV. It was one of the first reports in the Rio Grande Valley 'Big Bird' scare. A video later showed a 'Big Bird' to be a great blue heron.
big-bird|Harlingen New Year sighting.source_title: The Texas-sized 'monster' bird that created a huge flap back in 1975 - San Antonio Current

big-bird|Armando Grimaldo attack.summary: Around 14 January 1976 Raymondville resident Armando Grimaldo said he was sitting outside when something with huge flapping wings attacked him from above, scratching him and tearing his clothes. He was taken to the Willacy County hospital in shock. Wildlife experts suggested large birds such as storks or herons for the wave of sightings.
big-bird|Armando Grimaldo attack.source_title: The Texas-sized 'monster' bird that created a huge flap back in 1975 - San Antonio Current

big-grey-man|Collie's summit encounter.summary: Mountaineer and professor J. Norman Collie said that in 1891, walking down from the cairn on Ben Macdui in mist, he heard crunching footsteps behind him, as if something took one step for every three or four of his. Seized with terror, he ran for miles. Suggested explanations include the Brocken spectre, an optical effect seen on misty mountains.

big-grey-man|Collie tells the story publ.summary: In 1925 J. Norman Collie publicly described his 1891 experience of terror and giant footsteps on Ben Macdui. It is the first recorded account of the Big Grey Man, and other climbers later shared similar stories of footsteps and dread on the mountain.

big-grey-man|Peter Densham rescue-work e.summary: Peter Densham, doing mountain rescue work in the Cairngorms in 1945, said mist closed in, he heard strange noises and felt pressure around his neck, and he fled before seeing anything. His friend, climber Richard Frere, later described his own sense of 'a Presence' on the mountain.

bigfoot|Bluff Creek footprints.summary: In 1958 bulldozer operator Jerry Crew found 16-inch human-like footprints around logging equipment in Humboldt County, California. The Humboldt Times wrote about them and the name 'Bigfoot' spread nationwide. In 2002 the family of Crew's late co-worker Ray Wallace showed carved wooden feet and said Wallace had made the tracks.

bigfoot|Patterson-Gimlin film.summary: On 20 October 1967 Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin filmed about a minute of footage at Bluff Creek, California, showing a large, dark, hairy figure walking away and glancing back at the camera. It remains the most famous Bigfoot evidence. Skeptics argue it shows a man in an ape suit; neither filmmaker admitted a hoax and it has never been proven either way.

bigfoot|Ape Canyon attack.summary: In July 1924 a group of miners said 'ape-men' threw rocks at their cabin on Mount St. Helens all night after one of them shot at a creature. Forest Service rangers who visited found nothing and showed how the footprints could be faked. Decades later, a local man claimed he and friends had pranked the miners.

bigfoot|Skookum cast.summary: On 22 September 2000 researchers filming a TV show left fruit in a muddy wallow in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest and returned to find a large partial body print, which they cast in plaster. Some Bigfoot researchers say it shows a sitting primate, while scientific analysis says it was most likely made by a resting elk.

black-eyed-children|Brian Bethel encount.summary: In 1996 Texas reporter Brian Bethel posted to an online ghost mailing list that two children with entirely black eyes had approached his car in Abilene and asked to be let in. His story spread widely and is now seen as the start of the black-eyed children legend, often treated as a classic creepypasta. No evidence has ever supported it.

black-eyed-children|UK tabloid wave.summary: In one week of September 2014 the Daily Star ran three front-page stories about black-eyed children, linked to the sale of a supposedly haunted pub in Staffordshire, and claimed a worldwide rise in sightings. The coverage was sensational and no evidence was produced.

black-shuck|Bungay and Blythburgh church.summary: On 4 August 1577, amid thunder, a black dog was said to burst into churches at Bungay and Blythburgh in Suffolk, killing worshippers. At Blythburgh the steeple fell through the roof, and scorch marks on the north door are still called 'the devil's fingerprints'. Abraham Fleming's pamphlet A Straunge and Terrible Wunder spread the story.

black-shuck|First printed as \"Black Shu.summary: The name 'Black Shuck' first appears in print in an 1850 issue of Notes and Queries, where the Rev. E. S. Taylor described 'Shuck the Dog-fiend', a huge black shaggy dog with fiery eyes that many people in East Norfolk said they had seen in churchyards at midnight.

bloop|NOAA hydrophones record the Bloop.summary: In 1997 NOAA underwater microphones picked up a loud, very low-frequency sound, nicknamed the Bloop, roughly located at 50°S 100°W in the remote South Pacific. It was once suggested to be a huge animal. By 2012 NOAA described it as consistent with icequakes from glaciers, such as ice breaking off or scraping the seabed.

bukit-timah-monkey-man|First claimed sig.summary: The first report of the Bukit Timah Monkey Man is said to date to about 1805, when a Malay elder described an upright-walking creature with a monkey-like face in the Bukit Timah area. The account comes from folklore and has never been verified.

bukit-timah-monkey-man|New Paper sightin.summary: In 2007 the Singapore tabloid The New Paper ran a series of stories gathering accounts from people who said they had seen the monkey man in the Bukit Timah area. None of the reports was backed by photos or physical evidence.

bukit-timah-monkey-man|Night hiker repor.summary: In late 2020 a night hiker in the Bukit Timah area reported seeing the creature, and the claim was widely covered in local media. No photo or evidence confirmed it; some suggest local long-tailed macaques may account for such sightings.

bunnyman|Hatchet thrown through a parked.summary: On 19 October 1970 an Air Force Academy cadet and his fiancée, parked on Guinea Road in Burke, Virginia, said a man in a white suit with bunny ears shouted that they were trespassing and threw a hatchet through their car window. Police examined the hatchet but had no leads, and the case was closed. Library archivist Brian Conley later traced this as one of the two real incidents behind the legend.

bunnyman|Man in rabbit costume chops at.summary: On 31 October 1970 a construction security guard on Guinea Road in Burke, Virginia, said a man in a grey, black and white bunny costume began chopping at the porch post of an unfinished house with a long-handled axe, complaining about trespassers, then ran into the woods. No one was caught. It is the second documented incident behind the Bunny Man legend.

bunyip|Murrumbidgee skull.summary: In January 1846 a settler took a strange skull from the banks of the Murrumbidgee River near Balranald, and local Aboriginal people reportedly called it a bunyip. It drew crowds when shown at the Australian Museum in Sydney. Experts including Richard Owen identified it as the deformed skull of a foal or calf.

cadborosaurus|Naden Harbour carcass.summary: In October 1937 workers at the Naden Harbour whaling station on Haida Gwaii found a long, snake-like carcass in the stomach of a sperm whale and photographed it. Some believe it was a young Cadborosaurus. A sample sent to the BC Provincial Museum was tentatively identified as a fetal baleen whale.

cattle-mutilation|Snippy the horse.summary: In September 1967 a horse widely reported as 'Snippy' was found dead near Alamosa, Colorado, with the flesh stripped from its head and neck. Newspapers nationwide ran the story in October 1967 with headlines linking it to flying saucers, starting the modern cattle-mutilation idea. Mainstream experts concluded the horse died of natural causes.

cattle-mutilation|Rommel investigation b.summary: In May 1979 retired FBI agent Kenneth Rommel began a federally funded investigation into livestock mutilations in New Mexico. His 297-page report, released in June 1980, concluded that the mutilations were mostly the result of normal predators and scavengers. Some local investigators disputed his findings.

champ|Mansi photograph.summary: In 1977 Sandra Mansi, on vacation with her family, took a photograph at Lake Champlain that appears to show a long neck and head rising from the water. It is the best-known image of Champ. Critics note the bay is shallow and suggest a rising log; Mansi said she had thrown away the negative and could not find the spot again, so the photo could not be verified.

chessie|Perch fishermen sighting.summary: In 1943 two perch fishermen near Baltimore reported seeing a strange creature in the water, according to the book Weird Maryland. It is one of the earliest accounts of the Chesapeake Bay monster later nicknamed Chessie. Nothing more was confirmed.

chessie|Frew video.summary: In 1982 Robert and Karen Frew videotaped a long, brownish object moving through the water off Kent Island, Maryland, which they said was Chessie. The object was never identified, and the video remains the best-known Chessie evidence.

chessie|Magothy River roadside report.summary: On 5 April 2014 a Maryland man said that while parked beside the Magothy River at high tide he saw a black, snake-like creature 25 to 30 feet long moving just under the surface a few feet from his car. It is one of the most recent reported Chessie sightings and was not confirmed.

chupacabra|Canóvanas attacks.summary: In 1995 dead sheep and other animals with puncture wounds were reported across Puerto Rico. In August a Canóvanas resident described a strange creature, and the town became the centre of the scare, with claims of up to 150 animals killed. Investigator Benjamin Radford later concluded her description closely matched the alien in the 1995 film Species.

chupacabra|Cuero carcass.summary: In 2007 a rancher near Cuero, Texas, preserved a strange hairless carcass she believed had killed her chickens and called it a chupacabra. Experts from Texas State University tested the DNA and found it was a coyote.

crop-circles|Tully saucer nest.summary: In 1966 a farmer near Tully, Queensland, said he saw a saucer-shaped craft rise from a swamp and fly away, leaving a flattened circle of reeds. The 'saucer nest' became the most famous early case. British pranksters Doug Bower and Dave Chorley later said it inspired them to start making crop circles.

crop-circles|Bower and Chorley reveal th.summary: In 1991 Doug Bower and Dave Chorley told the press they had been making crop circles in southern England since 1978 and showed reporters how they did it, claiming more than 200 circles. Their confession made clear that crop circles are man-made, though new formations kept appearing.

crop-circles|Milk Hill formation.summary: In August 2001 a huge spiral pattern made of about 400 circles appeared in a wheat field at Milk Hill, near Alton Barnes in Wiltshire. It was one of the largest and most complex crop formations recorded. Like other formations, it is widely considered the work of human circle makers.
crop-circles|Milk Hill formation.source_title: Crop circles make a comeback - Farmers Weekly

dingonek|John Alfred Jordan fires at the.summary: In 1907 big-game hunter John Alfred Jordan said that on the Maggori (Migori) River near Lake Victoria he saw a water beast with leopard markings, armadillo-like scales and two long fangs, fired a rifle at it, and fled when it leapt from the water. The story is known only from fellow hunter Edgar Beecher Bronson's 1910 memoir In Closed Territory, and no specimen was ever found.

dobhar-chu|Glenade Lough attack.summary: Local tradition says that in 1722 Grace Connolly was killed by a dobhar-chú, a giant otter-like 'water hound', while washing clothes at Glenade Lough, and that her husband killed the creature. A headstone in Conwall cemetery is said to mark her grave and shows a carved animal. The story is local folklore; the carved animal on the stone looks like a dog with a tufted tail.

dogman|\"The Legend\" broadcast.summary: On 1 April 1987 Steve Cook, a DJ at WTCM-FM in Traverse City, played a song he had recorded called 'The Legend' about a dog-headed creature, as an April Fools' joke. Listeners began calling in with their own sightings and it became the station's most requested song. Cook has since received more than 100 reports, and the 'Dogman' name stuck.

dogman|Beast of Bray Road.summary: In 1991 reporter Linda Godfrey began covering reports of a wolf-like creature, sometimes seen walking upright, along Bray Road near Elkhorn, Wisconsin. Her articles and later book linked it to the wider Dogman legend. Skeptics suggest witnesses saw wolves, large dogs or bears with mange.

dover-demon|Bartlett sighting.summary: On 21 April 1977 Bill Bartlett, then 17, said he saw a small creature with a large watermelon-shaped head and glowing orange eyes on a stone wall in Dover, Massachusetts. Two other local teens reported something similar over the next day. Police suspected a school-vacation hoax; others suggest a foal, moose calf or owl.

ebu-gogo|Homo floresiensis fossils found.summary: In 2003 an Australian-Indonesian team found the remains of a tiny human species in Liang Bua cave on Flores, named Homo floresiensis and nicknamed 'hobbits'. The find revived interest in the local ebu gogo stories of small hairy people. Later dating to about 50,000 years ago weakened the idea that the ebu gogo tales preserve memories of the species.

emela-ntouka|Blancou's report in Mammali.note: Could not open or verify Lucien Blancou's 1954 Mammalia paper or any reliable page describing it; the Wikipedia article 'Emela-ntouka' no longer exists (404) and the Mokele-mbembe article does not mention Blancou.

emela-ntouka|Mackal expeditions.summary: In 1980 and 1981 University of Chicago biologist Roy Mackal led expeditions to the Likouala region of the Republic of the Congo to look for mokele-mbembe. He did not see any creature, but collected local accounts, including stories of the emela-ntouka, a large horned animal said to kill elephants. No physical evidence was found.

enfield-monster|McDaniel encounter.summary: On the night of 25 April 1973 Henry McDaniel of Enfield, Illinois, said a grey creature about 4½ feet tall with three legs and large pink eyes was outside his door. He fired at it and said it hissed and bounded away. Police found dog-like tracks, and suggestions ranged from an escaped ape or kangaroo to a hoax.

fairies|Robert Kirk writes The Secret Co.summary: Robert Kirk, minister of Aberfoyle, wrote The Secret Commonwealth around 1691, describing Highland beliefs about fairies and second sight as if they were natural facts. He died in 1692 before publishing it; local legend says the fairies took him. Walter Scott first published it in 1815.

fairies|Murder of Bridget Cleary, said t.summary: In March 1895 Bridget Cleary of Ballyvadlea, County Tipperary, was killed by her husband Michael, who claimed the sick woman had been replaced by a fairy changeling. Her body was burned and buried. He was convicted of manslaughter and served fifteen years, and the case drew huge press attention in Ireland and Britain.

fairies|Cottingley Fairies photographs (.summary: In 1917 cousins Elsie Wright and Frances Griffiths took photos in Cottingley, near Bradford, that seemed to show them with fairies. Arthur Conan Doyle promoted them as genuine in 1920. In the early 1980s the women admitted they used cardboard cut-outs copied from a children's book, though Frances maintained the fifth photo was real.

fairies|Latoon fairy bush saved from the.summary: In 1999 storyteller Eddie Lenihan protested plans to cut down a whitethorn at Latoon, County Clare, for a new road, saying it was a meeting place of Munster fairies. The campaign made international news and the road plans were changed so the bush was spared.

flathead-lake-monster|U.S. Grant steambo.summary: The first reported sighting is said to date to 1889, when Captain James C. Kerr of the steamboat U.S. Grant and his passengers saw a large, whale-like object in Flathead Lake. One passenger reportedly shot at it and it dived. The account comes from later local retellings.

flatwoods-monster|Fisher farm encounter.summary: On 12 September 1952 a group of local boys and adults in Flatwoods, West Virginia, followed a bright light that seemed to land on a farm and said they saw a tall figure with a head like the ace of spades that hissed and glided toward them, and smelled a pungent mist. Investigator Joe Nickell later suggested a meteor, aircraft lights and a barn owl in a tree.

fouke-monster|Ford family encounter.summary: In early May 1971 Bobby and Elizabeth Ford said a large hairy creature reached through a window of their rented house near Fouke, Arkansas, and that the men fired shots at it. Three-toed tracks and scratches on the porch were found, but no blood. The case inspired the 1972 film The Legend of Boggy Creek.

fresno-nightcrawlers|First security came.summary: In 2007 a home security camera in south Fresno, California, recorded what appeared to be white figures shaped like a pair of legs without a torso walking across a yard. The clip aired on Univision and spread online; what it shows has never been explained.

fresno-nightcrawlers|Yosemite Lakes Park.summary: In 2011 more security footage from Yosemite Lakes Park, California, appeared to show similar leg-like white figures. A TV show tried to test whether it was faked and called the result inconclusive, and the 'nightcrawler' name comes from that program.

gambo|Owen Burnham finds the carcass.summary: On 12 June 1983 a young British wildlife enthusiast, Owen Burnham, found a 15-foot carcass with a long toothed beak and four flippers on Bungalow Beach in Kotu, The Gambia. Two fishermen were cutting off its head to sell to a tourist. Its identity is still debated, with beaked whales among the suggestions.

gef|Irving family report a talking anima.summary: In September 1931 the Irving family of Cashen's Gap, near Dalby on the Isle of Man, said a talking creature that called itself Gef, a mongoose born in India, lived in the wooden walls of their farmhouse. The story became a press sensation, though almost no outsiders saw it. Many investigators concluded it was a hoax using ventriloquism.

gef|Harry Price and Richard Lambert inve.summary: In July 1935 ghost hunter Harry Price and Richard Lambert, editor of The Listener, visited the farm and later wrote The Haunting of Cashen's Gap (1936). Hair said to be Gef's was identified as dog hair, possibly from the family sheepdog, and supposed paw prints matched no mongoose. They found little to impress them.

ghost-rockets|First reports.summary: On 26 February 1946 observers in Finland reported rocket-like objects in the sky, the first of the 'ghost rocket' reports. About 2,000 sightings followed across Scandinavia that year, especially in Sweden. Many were later put down to meteors, while others were suspected Soviet missile tests; some remain unexplained.

ghost-rockets|Lake Kölmjärv crash.summary: On 19 July 1946 witnesses in northern Sweden said a grey, rocket-shaped object with wings crashed into Lake Kölmjärv. A three-week Swedish military search found that the lake bottom had been disturbed but recovered nothing. The officer in charge suggested the object may have been made of a light material that disintegrated.

globster|St. Augustine Monster found on.summary: In late 1896 two boys found a huge mass of tough tissue on Anastasia Island near St. Augustine, Florida, and local physician DeWitt Webb examined it. It was long promoted as a giant octopus. A 1995 analysis concluded it was a large mass of whale blubber, probably from a sperm whale.

globster|Tasmanian Globster washes ashor.summary: In August 1960 a 20-foot mass with no eyes or obvious bones washed ashore north of the Interview River in western Tasmania. It inspired Ivan Sanderson to coin the word 'globster'. In 1981 it was identified as the remains of a whale.

globster|Chilean blob found on Pinuno Be.summary: In July 2003 a 12-metre, 13-tonne mass of tissue washed ashore on Pinuno Beach in Los Muermos, Chile, sparking talk of an unknown giant octopus. In 2004 DNA tests showed it was the remains of a sperm whale, a mass of fatty tissue left after the carcass decayed.

gnomes|Sir Charles Isham begins the gnom.summary: Sir Charles Isham, who inherited Lamport Hall in Northamptonshire in 1846, built a large rockery and filled it with terracotta gnome figures brought from Germany, which is credited with starting the British garden gnome tradition. One original gnome survives and is on display at the hall.

goatman|Folklore project records the leg.summary: In May 1971 a University of Maryland student completed a folklore project on the Goatman, a half-man, half-goat said to haunt Tucker Road in Fort Washington, Maryland. The paper went into the Maryland Folklife Archives and is the earliest documented record of the legend.

goatman|Newspaper places him on Fletcher.summary: In October 1971 reporter Karen Hosler found the folklore project in the archives and wrote it up for the Prince George's County News, placing the Goatman near Fletchertown Road in Bowie. Around then a dog's death was blamed on the creature by residents, helping the legend spread among local teenagers.

grafton-monster|Cockrell sighting.summary: Late on 16 June 1964 Grafton Sentinel reporter Robert Cockrell said he saw a tall, pale, seal-like figure with no obvious head beside Route 119 near the Tygart Valley River. Groups of locals went hunting for it, and within days the paper put the episode down to 'spring fever' and imagination.

grafton-monster|First Grafton Monster Fe.summary: In June 2024, around the 60th anniversary of the 1964 sightings, Grafton, West Virginia, held its first Grafton Monster Festival. Coverage mentioned pop-up displays and plans for a related museum, as the town embraced the creature for tourism.

grassman|Minerva Monster sightings.summary: In August 1978 members of a family near Minerva, in Stark County, Ohio, and others reported a large, hairy, upright creature, and the sheriff's office became involved. The 'Minerva Monster' got wide press coverage. Nothing was found, and the case was revisited in a 2015 documentary.

grassman|Salt Fork reports begin to pile.summary: Since the mid-1980s nearly 40 reports of a large, hairy, upright creature have been logged around Salt Fork State Park and Lake in Guernsey County, Ohio. The park now hosts the annual Ohio Bigfoot Conference, started in 2005. None of the reports has been confirmed.
grassman|Salt Fork reports begin to pile.source_title: Bigfoot adventures afoot in southeast Ohio - The Marietta Times

green-fireballs|Pilot sightings.summary: On 5 December 1948 two aircraft crews over New Mexico, one civilian and one military, reported a bright green 'ball of fire' crossing the sky, and pilots reported more in the following days. Meteorite expert Lincoln LaPaz of the University of New Mexico, who saw one himself, argued they were not normal meteors.

green-fireballs|Los Alamos fireball conf.summary: In February 1949 military officers and scientists, including Edward Teller and Joseph Kaplan, met at Los Alamos to discuss the green fireballs seen over New Mexico's nuclear sites. They could not identify them. A monitoring effort, Project Twinkle, followed but was dropped without firm results.

grey-aliens|Betty and Barney Hill encoun.summary: Betty and Barney Hill said that in September 1961, driving through New Hampshire's White Mountains, they were taken aboard a craft by grey-skinned beings with large eyes. When their story became public in 1965, it helped fix the image of the 'grey' alien. Critics note possible influence from a TV episode aired shortly before Barney's hypnosis.

grey-aliens|Communion published.summary: In 1987 horror novelist Whitley Strieber published Communion, describing what he believed were encounters with beings he called 'visitors'. Hypnotist Budd Hopkins suggested his memories pointed to an alien encounter. The book was a bestseller for six months and was filmed in 1989 with Christopher Walken.

grootslang|Treasure hunter Peter Grayson.summary: In 1917 English businessman Peter Grayson went looking for treasure in the Richtersveld of South Africa. After lions attacked and injured members of his party, he disappeared, and rumours spread that the grootslang, a huge serpent of local legend, had taken him. No trace of him was found.

hibagon|First wave of sightings.summary: From 1970 people around Mount Hiba in Hiroshima Prefecture began reporting a short, ape-like creature with a dark face and brown hair, which the press named the Hibagon. Sightings caused a local sensation, but no physical evidence was ever found.

hibagon|Sazawa and Harada reports.summary: A 1972 report describes two sightings, by a Mr. Sazawa and a Mrs. Harada, of a creature with a chocolate-brown face, brown hair and deep, glaring eyes. In both cases it fled from armed residents who were hunting it. The sightings were never confirmed.

hinzelmann|Hinzelmann's haunting begins.summary: According to a book based on a local pastor's diary, a household spirit called Hinzelmann began haunting Hudemühlen Castle in Lower Saxony in 1584. First heard as knocking, it later talked with servants, did kitchen chores and played tricks, then left of its own accord in 1588. The story was retold by the Brothers Grimm.

hobyahs|Tale from a Perth family printed.summary: 'The Hobyahs', a tale of goblin-like creatures who come at night, was sent by S. V. Proudfit of Washington, D.C., who credited a family from Perth, Scotland, and printed in the Journal of American Folklore (vol. 4, 1891). Joseph Jacobs later included it in More English Fairy Tales. It is a folk tale, not a sighting.

hodag|Shepard \"kills\" a hodag.summary: In 1893 Rhinelander newspapers reported that a group led by timber cruiser and known prankster Eugene Shepard had found and killed a hodag, a beast with a frog's head, an elephant's grin and spikes down its back, using dynamite. It was a prank, and the hodag went on to become Rhinelander's mascot.

hodag|Live hodag shown at the fair.summary: In 1896 Eugene Shepard said he had captured a live hodag by chloroforming it in its cave, and showed it at the first Oneida County fair, moving it with hidden wires. Thousands came to see it. When Smithsonian scientists announced they would come to inspect it, Shepard admitted it was a hoax.

honey-island-swamp-monster|Harlan Ford s.summary: In 1963 Harlan Ford, a retired air traffic controller and amateur wildlife photographer, said he saw a tall, hairy creature in Louisiana's Honey Island Swamp. In 1974 he and a friend reported odd footprints and a dead boar. A film reel found after his death in 1980 is said to show the creature; a TV show later recreated it with a man in a ghillie suit.

hook-island-sea-monster|Robert Le Serrec.summary: In December 1964 Robert Le Serrec, with his family and a friend, said they photographed a huge tadpole-like creature in Stonehaven Bay at Hook Island, Queensland. The best-known photo circulated around the world. No other evidence was ever produced.

hoop-snake|Described in a travel letter.summary: A letter from 1784, published in London in Tour in the U.S.A., describes the hoop snake, said to grab its tail in its mouth and roll after its victims like a wheel. It is one of the earliest written records of this American folk belief. No snake actually does this.

hopkinsville-goblins|Sutton farmhouse si.summary: On the night of 21-22 August 1955 members of two families at the Sutton farmhouse near Kelly, Kentucky, told police that small, glowing creatures had attacked the house for hours and they had fired at them. Police and military investigators found bullet holes but no other evidence. The Air Force's Project Blue Book filed it as a hoax, and skeptic Joe Nickell suggested great horned owls.

huldufolk|Bulldozer trouble blamed on el.summary: During road construction in Kópavogur in 1971, a bulldozer broke down and the driver blamed elves living in a large rock. Newspapers ran with the story, helping start the popular idea that elves often hold up road building in Iceland. The street is now called Álfhólsvegur, 'Elf Hill Road'.

huldufolk|Group searches for elves at th.summary: In 1982 about 150 Icelanders went to the NATO base at Keflavík to look for elves who might be endangered by American jets and AWACS planes. It was a well-known example of how hidden-people beliefs mixed with protest in Iceland.

huldufolk|Rockfall on residential street.summary: In 2011 rocks crashed down onto residential streets in Bolungarvík, and some locals blamed the hidden people. It is one of several modern incidents tied to huldufólk beliefs.

huldufolk|Road through the Gálgahraun la.summary: In 2013 work on a road from the Álftanes peninsula to Garðabær through the Gálgahraun lava field was halted when environmental groups and people who believe in elves protested. The Road Administration said it treated hidden-people beliefs as part of Iceland's cultural heritage.

igopogo|Soules sighting.summary: Early settler David Soules is credited with the first reported Igopogo sighting in 1823: while tending sheep near Lake Simcoe, he said he saw a long creature leaving a wake in the water and a trail in the mud. The account is unconfirmed.

igopogo|Chief Wellington Charles sightin.summary: In 1952 four witnesses, including Wellington Charles, chief of the Georgina Island First Nation, reported a large creature in Lake Simcoe. It is one of the best-known Igopogo sightings and was reported in the Globe and Mail.

igopogo|Sonar contact.summary: In 1983 sonar operator William Skrypetz said his equipment showed a large animal with a long neck in Lake Simcoe. Others argued the reading was more likely a school of fish.

igopogo|Seal-like animal video.summary: In 1991 a video was recorded at Lake Simcoe said to show 'a large, seal-like animal'. It is among the few recorded images linked to the Igopogo, and the animal was never identified.

indrid-cold|Derenberger roadside encount.summary: Woodrow Derenberger said that on 2 November 1966, driving on Interstate 77 near Parkersburg, West Virginia, a lamp-shaped craft blocked the road and a smiling man in a shiny dark coat, who called himself Cold, spoke to him by telepathy. He told his story at a press conference and on TV the next day, and later claimed trips to the planet 'Lanulos'.

inkanyamba|Game ranger reports a horse-h.summary: In 1962 a game ranger named Buthelezi said he saw an animal with a horse-like head and a serpent's body basking on a sandbank in the Umgeni River, which he took to be the inkanyamba of Zulu tradition. Later reports in the area are suspected to be crocodiles, large eels or tourism stunts.

issie|About twenty people see a two-hump.summary: In 1978 about twenty people at Lake Ikeda in Kagoshima reported a large black creature with two humps swimming in the lake, and a local man took a photo. The sightings created the 'Issie' legend. The lake is known to hold large eels up to about six feet long.

jackalope|Herrick brothers mount the fir.summary: According to The New York Times, in 1932 Douglas Herrick of Douglas, Wyoming, and his brother, both amateur taxidermists, put deer antlers on a jackrabbit carcass and created the first jackalope mount. They sold it for $10 to a local hotel, and the joke animal became a symbol of Douglas and the American West.

jenny-haniver|Conrad Gesner pictures one.summary: In 1558 Swiss naturalist Conrad Gesner published the earliest known picture of a Jenny Haniver, in volume IV of his Historia Animalium. He warned readers that these 'dragons' and 'basilisks' were really dried rays that had been cut and shaped by people, not real monsters.

jersey-devil|Phenomenal Week.summary: During the week of 16-23 January 1909, newspapers printed hundreds of reports of the Jersey Devil from across South Jersey and the Philadelphia area, including strange hoof prints in the snow and claimed attacks on a trolley and a social club. Police in Camden and Bristol said they fired at it. Historians see it as a classic case of mass hysteria fed by newspapers and some hoaxes.

kappa|Tōno Monogatari folk tales, includ.summary: In 1910 folklorist Kunio Yanagita published Tōno Monogatari, a collection of legends from Tōno in Iwate Prefecture that includes several tales of kappa, mischievous water spirits. The town's Kappabuchi pool behind Jōken-ji temple is still said to be home to kappa and is a popular sight.

knockers|Herbert Hoover writes to Grass.summary: In 1963 former president Herbert Hoover, who began his mining career at Grass Valley, answered a request from the town's Fourth of July committee, which chose tommyknockers as its theme. He described them as gnomes that helped hard-rock miners by warning of rock falls, and said a statue of a mine gnome guarded his apartment door.
knockers|Herbert Hoover writes to Grass.source_title: Herbert Hoover and the Tommyknockers: Mythic Gnomes of the Mine Shafts - Hoover Heads (Hoover Presidential Library blog)

knockers|Tommyknocker Brewery named afte.summary: Tommyknocker Brewery in Idaho Springs, Colorado, which began serving in 1994, is named after the knockers, the little mine spirits that Cornish miners brought with them to American mining towns. The name keeps the old mining legend alive in a former gold-rush town.

kobold|Hinzelmann begins haunting Hudemü.summary: According to a book drawn from a local pastor's diary, the kobold Hinzelmann began haunting Hudemühlen Castle in Lower Saxony in 1584. Usually invisible, it talked with servants, cleaned the kitchen, punished rudeness and could take the form of a feather or a marten, before leaving in 1588.

kobold|Ernst Weyden writes down the Hein.summary: In 1826 Ernst Weyden recorded the Cologne legend of the Heinzelmännchen, little house spirits who secretly did the townspeople's work at night until a curious tailor's wife scattered peas to trip them, and they left for good. August Kopisch's 1836 poem made the story famous.

kongamato|Melland's account.summary: In his 1923 book In Witch-Bound Africa, Frank Melland wrote that the Kaonde people described the kongamato, a red, featherless flying creature with teeth said to overturn boats in the Jiundu swamp. When shown pictures, they reportedly picked out a pterosaur. Suggestions include a giant bat or a bird such as the saddle-billed stork.

kraken|Pontoppidan describes the kraken.summary: Bishop Erik Pontoppidan of Bergen described the kraken in his Natural History of Norway (1752-53), drawing on fishermen's stories of a creature so vast it could be mistaken for islands. His work spread the kraken legend in the English-speaking world. Modern writers link it to sightings of giant squid.

kraken|Giant squid reportedly attacks a.summary: In 1873 two men fishing for herring in Conception Bay, Newfoundland, met a huge creature with a beak and long tentacles that spewed ink. Fisherman Theophilus Piccot hacked off tentacles with a hatchet before it escaped, and the evidence helped prove that giant squid are real.

kraken|First photographs of a live giant.summary: On 30 September 2004 Japanese researchers Tsunemi Kubodera and Kyoichi Mori photographed a live giant squid about 900 metres down off the Ogasawara Islands, using a baited line with a camera. The pictures, released in 2005, were the first of a live giant squid in its natural habitat.

kraken|First video of a giant squid in i.summary: In July 2012 a team from Japan's NHK and the Discovery Channel, using crewed submersibles near the Ogasawara Islands, filmed a live giant squid about 3 metres long in the deep sea. The footage, aired in early 2013, was the first video of the animal in its natural habitat.

labynkyr-devil|Geologist Viktor Tverdokh.summary: In 1953 Soviet geologist Viktor Tverdokhlebov wrote about a creature said to live in remote Lake Labynkyr in Yakutia, noting theories of a giant pike or a relic reptile and that bones and jaws of some animal had been found. It is the earliest written mention of the 'Labynkyr Devil'. Nothing was confirmed.

labynkyr-devil|Expedition makes a record.summary: In March 2013 a Russian Geographical Society expedition dived under the ice of Lake Labynkyr to take water and soil samples in extreme cold. They found no sign of a monster, and scientists noted the lake could not support a breeding population of large animals.

lagarfljot-worm|Annals record a marvel i.summary: Icelandic annals record a 'marvel' seen in Lagarfljót in 1345: humps or island-like shapes rising from the water far apart, with no head or tail seen. It is generally counted as the first sighting of the Lagarfljót Worm.

lagarfljot-worm|Forestry chief sighting.summary: In 1963 Sigurður Blöndal, head of the Icelandic Forest Service, reported seeing something unusual in Lagarfljót. His standing made it one of the most cited modern sightings of the worm. No explanation was confirmed.

lagarfljot-worm|Viral video.summary: In February 2012 RÚV, Iceland's national broadcaster, aired a video appearing to show a long shape swimming in the icy river near Egilsstaðir. Frame-by-frame analysis showed it made no forward progress, suggesting an object such as a frozen fishing net moved by current. A local panel still voted 7-6 to declare it authentic.

lake-tianchi-monster|Buffalo-like creatu.summary: The first reported sighting at Heaven Lake (Tianchi), on the China-North Korea border, dates to 1903, when a large buffalo-like creature was said to attack three people and then retreat into the water after being shot six times. The story is unverified.

lake-tianchi-monster|Telescope sighting.summary: In August 1962 a person watching Heaven Lake through a telescope reportedly saw two creatures chasing each other in the water, and more than a hundred people reported sightings around that time. No animals were identified.

lake-tianchi-monster|TV reporter films s.summary: On 6 September 2007 Chinese TV reporter Zhuo Yongsheng said he filmed six unidentified creatures swimming in pairs in Heaven Lake and sent still photos to the Xinhua news agency. The images show shapes leaving ripples; the animals were never identified.

lake-van-monster|Saadet newspaper says a.summary: On 29 April 1889 the Ottoman newspaper Saadet reported that a creature had dragged a man into Lake Van. The government sent a survey team to the lake, but it did not find the animal.

lake-van-monster|Ünal Kozak films an all.summary: In 1997 local man Ünal Kozak released video he said showed a large creature in Lake Van, and it was widely reported. Critics asked whether the frame hid a boat and noted the steady bubbling looked like an air hose. Some locals called the monster story a commercial ploy.

lake-worth-monster|Summer of sightings a.summary: In July 1969 people at Lake Worth near Fort Worth, Texas, reported a hairy 'half-man, half-goat' creature that reportedly jumped onto a car and threw a tire at a crowd. Police found no evidence. The sightings stopped when school resumed, and many suspected pranks by students.

lake-worth-monster|Prank confession lett.summary: In 2005 a reporter at the Fort Worth Star-Telegram received an anonymous letter from someone saying he and two high school friends decided to 'scare people' at the lake in 1969 using a tinfoil mask. The writer's identity was never confirmed.

lizard-man|Christopher Davis encounter.summary: In July 1988 Christopher Davis, 17, told the Lee County sheriff that two weeks earlier, after fixing a flat tyre near Scape Ore Swamp outside Bishopville, South Carolina, a 7-foot green, scaly creature with red eyes jumped on his car. The story made national news. Skeptic Ben Radford found that Davis's account changed many times and called it incredible.
lizard-man|Christopher Davis encounter.source_title: Lizard Man of Scape Ore Swamp - Wikipedia

loch-ness-monster|Mackay sighting.summary: On 15 April 1933 Aldie Mackay and her husband, driving along the loch, said they saw a huge whale-like creature rolling in the water. Alex Campbell wrote it up in The Inverness Courier on 2 May 1933, and the story brought the 'monster' worldwide attention. Scientists explain such sightings as misidentified animals or objects, wishful thinking or hoaxes.

loch-ness-monster|Surgeon's Photograph.summary: In April 1934 a photo credited to London gynaecologist Robert Kenneth Wilson appeared to show a small head and long neck rising from Loch Ness. It became the most famous Nessie image. Since 1994 it has been widely accepted as a hoax: a toy submarine with a model head, built by Christian Spurling, stepson of big-game hunter Marmaduke Wetherell, who admitted it in 1991.

loch-ness-monster|Loch Ness eDNA survey.summary: In June 2018 a team led by Prof. Neil Gemmell of the University of Otago sampled environmental DNA throughout Loch Ness. Results published in 2019 showed no reptile, shark, sturgeon or catfish DNA, but a large amount of eel DNA. Gemmell said very large eels could not be ruled out, though none have been found.

loveland-frog|Police sightings.summary: Early on 3 March 1972 Loveland, Ohio, police officer Ray Shockey said a frog-like animal about 3 to 4 feet long crossed Riverside Drive and climbed over the guardrail toward the Little Miami River. Weeks later a second officer shot a similar animal and in 2016 said it was a large iguana missing its tail.

lukwata|C. W. Hobley records Lukwata sto.summary: In 1913 British colonial administrator C. W. Hobley wrote that peoples on both sides of Lake Victoria told stories of the Lukwata, a large water creature said to attack fishing canoes. There is no scientific evidence for it, but it remains part of Baganda tradition.

lusca|Diver George Benjamin's National G.summary: In a 1970 National Geographic article, diver George Benjamin described exploring the blue holes of Andros in the Bahamas and the local belief in the lusca, a half-shark, half-octopus said to drag victims into the holes. He never met one, but later articles and documentaries echoed the local belief.

makiawisug|Frank Speck publishes the Muh.summary: In 1903 anthropologist Frank Speck published 'Mohegan Traditions of Muhkeahweesug, the Little Men', based on what he learned from Fidelia Fielding, a respected Mohegan elder and the last fluent speaker of the Mohegan-Pequot language. The makiawisug are the Little People of Mohegan tradition.

mamlambo|Villagers blame drownings on a.summary: Between January and April 1997 villagers near Mount Ayliff in South Africa blamed up to nine drownings in the Mzintlava River on the mamlambo, described as a huge reptile with a horse-like head that glowed green at night. Police said the bodies had been damaged by crabs after drowning.

manipogo|McKay sighting.summary: In September 1909 Hudson's Bay Company fur trader Valentine McKay said he saw a huge creature in Cedar Lake near Graves Point on Lake Manitoba. It is counted as the first documented Manipogo sighting by a settler.

manipogo|Name coined after a wave of sig.summary: In 1960, after several sightings that year, the creature was named Manipogo by Tom Locke, a provincial land inspector, combining 'Manitoba' and 'Ogopogo'. University of Manitoba zoologist James McLeod later searched for remains but found none.

manipogo|Vincent and Konefell photo.summary: In August 1962 fishermen Richard Vincent and John Konefell said they saw a large snake-like creature about 60 yards from their boat near Meadow Portage on Lake Manitoba. Vincent's picture is the only photo ever produced from a Manipogo sighting.

mapinguari|Oren's ground sloth hypothesi.summary: In a 1993 paper, ornithologist David Oren suggested that stories of the mapinguari, a huge, foul-smelling forest creature, might come from encounters with a surviving giant ground sloth. He collected many hunter and rubber-tapper accounts, but no physical evidence has been found.

lechuza|Big Bird flap revives the legend.summary: In 1975 people walking county roads at night near Robstown, Texas, said a huge bird swooped at them, and the Corpus Christi Caller-Times covered the reports. When witnesses said it had a human face, people linked it to La Lechuza, the witch-owl of Mexican-American folklore. Further reports came from Banquete and Alice.
lechuza|Big Bird flap revives the legend.source_title: La Lechuza legend serves as both a cautionary tale and a story of revenge - Texas Standard

leprechaun|Cooley Mountains 'protected z.summary: Campaigners in Carlingford, County Louth, had Slieve Foy in the Cooley Mountains formally declared a 'Designated Area of Protection for Flora, Fauna, Wild Animals and Little People' under the EU Habitats Directive. The designation followed years of leprechaun-themed tourism started by a local businessman. Leprechauns are not a legally listed species.

bessie|1793 sloop captain's sighting.summary: The earliest Lake Erie serpent story dates to 1793: a ship's captain shooting ducks north of Sandusky, Ohio, said he startled a large snake-like creature 'more than a rod' (16½ feet) long. The account is unconfirmed, and later sightings from 1817 onward are better documented.
